opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really big commitment, and honestly it's the largest investment in alignment that I'm aware of anyone having made so far. If you think about how much compute OpenAI has secured, 20% of that is a lot. It's significantly more than what the field of alignment as a whole has had access to up until now. So when I look at it, I'm pretty happy that we got this.

That said, I want to be careful about how people interpret it. The commitment is 20% of the compute secured *to date*, so it isn't 20% of everything OpenAI will ever have. As the company scales up, that fraction of the total will shrink. But I don't think the right frame is "is this enough forever." The right question is whether it's enough to make serious progress on the problem over the next few years, and I think it gives us a very real shot.

It's also a strong signal. It tells people inside the company and outside that this problem is being taken seriously at the leadership level, and that alignment isn't something we'll get to once capabilities are done. Part of the point of the superalignment team is to show that you can put real resources behind this and turn it into a concrete research program with a deadline. We've said four years, and that's ambitious, but having the compute means compute shouldn't be the bottleneck. The bottleneck is going to be ideas and people.

So I'd say the compute is necessary but not sufficient. What matters now is whether we can use it well. That means finding the right research bets, building the automated alignment researcher we're aiming for, and getting really talented people to work on it. If you're listening and you think you could contribute, that's where I'd point you. We have the resources. What we need is more great people working on the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate refers to compute OpenAI has “secured,” but does not clarify that this includes both already accessible compute and compute covered by purchase orders.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a pretty big deal. When we were putting the superalignment team together, one of the things we really wanted was a commitment from the company that we'd actually have the resources to do the work, and 20% of the compute secured to date is a lot of compute. It's not a trivial number. If you think about how much compute OpenAI has access to, and how much it has committed to, 20% of that is probably the largest single investment in alignment that's been made anywhere, and I think that's a strong signal that the company is taking this seriously.

Now, I want to be a little careful about how people interpret this. It's not 20% of the compute at any given moment that we're going to be spending every day. It's 20% of what's been secured so far, over the next four years, and we can draw on it as we need it. So early on we won't be using that much, and later on, as we scale up our experiments and start training bigger models for alignment research, we'll use more. The point is that we don't have to fight for compute every time we want to run an experiment, and we're not competing with the product side or the capabilities side for every GPU.

The other thing I'd say is that compute is really important for the kind of alignment research we want to do, because a lot of the questions we care about are empirical. We want to run experiments with real models, train reward models, do scalable oversight experiments, study generalization, do interpretability on large models. All of that takes a lot of compute, and historically alignment research has been quite compute-starved relative to capabilities research. So having a serious budget changes the kind of questions you can ask.

Of course, compute by itself doesn't solve the problem. You still need the right people and the right ideas, and a lot of the hard work is figuring out what experiments are even worth running. But I think if you look at this commitment together with the goal of solving the core technical challenges of superintelligence alignment in four years, it tells you that this isn't a side project. It's something the company is betting a meaningful fraction of its resources on, and I think that's the right level of ambition given how fast things are moving.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a substantial commitment. Compute is one of the key resources you need to do this research, and committing a fifth of it gives you room to run experiments at a scale that would otherwise be difficult.

But compute alone doesn’t solve the problem. You also need great researchers and a research direction that actually works. So I’d view this as a commitment to making a serious attempt, rather than evidence that we’re going to succeed. Ultimately, what matters is whether we can use those resources to develop methods that reliably keep systems aligned as they become much more capable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really substantial commitment. Compute is one of the most valuable resources at OpenAI, and committing a fifth of it to this problem gives us room to do ambitious experiments. You can try things that might fail, and you can scale up approaches that look promising.

But compute alone doesn’t solve alignment. We still need good ideas, good people, and ways to tell whether we’re actually making progress. So I see it as a strong commitment of resources to tackling the problem, rather than a guarantee that we’ll succeed.
